name: Affinity bias
statement: People favour those who resemble them in background, interests or demography, and hiring and promotion decisions carry that preference.
meaning: Affinity bias is a term of corporate diversity training rather than of research psychology. A Crossref title search for the phrase returns behavioural finance, team-formation modelling, human-robot interaction, large language models and antibody chemistry. PubMed returns nine records, none of them a study of a construct by that name. What the term points at is covered by two older literatures that do have evidence behind them. The first is similarity-attraction, which Donn Byrne began measuring in 1961, and which holds that liking rises with similarity of attitudes. The second is in-group favouritism, which holds that people extend help and resources to members of their own category, and which has its own entry here. Affinity bias adds a third claim on top: that the preference operates inside workplace evaluation, unnoticed by the evaluator. That third claim is where the field evidence thins out.

origin.where: The Journal of Abnormal and Social Psychology
origin.note: No publication coining the name was located. Byrne's paper established the effect the name is applied to. The earliest indexed scholarly use of the exact phrase found in these searches is a 2012 chapter in a behavioural finance textbook, where it means an investor's preference for assets that flatter their self-image.

evidence:
Byrne's 1961 experiment is the root, and it is described here from Greenwald and Pettigrew's account rather than from Byrne. Subjects answered 26 attitude questions. Two weeks later they evaluated a stranger whose only visible property was a set of answers to those same questions, filled in by the experimenters to agree with the subject on all of them, most, few or none. Liking tracked agreement. Across six dependent measures, Greenwald and Pettigrew put the gap between the most and least similar strangers at a Cohen's d of 3.40. Rand and Wexley moved the design into hiring in 1975. They filmed a Black and a White applicant supplying biographical information that either matched a White interviewer's or did not, and had 160 raters score them. Biographical similarity raised ratings of job suitability. Neither applicant race nor the rater's need for affiliation produced a main effect, and prejudiced raters marked everybody down.

The strongest positive field result comes from personnel records rather than experiments. Giuliano, Levine and Leonard used the daily records of a large American retailer covering more than 700 stores, more than 1,500 store managers and more than 100,000 entry-level hires between February 1996 and July 1998. Manager turnover let them hold the store fixed. Under non-Black managers the probability that a new hire was Black fell by 3.5 to 4.0 percentage points, which in a typical store moves the Black share of hires from about 21 to 17 percent and the White share from 60 to 64 percent. In a typical southern store the same swap moved the Black share from 29 to 21 percent. Where Hispanics were at least 30 percent of the local population, replacing a Hispanic manager with a White one moved the Hispanic share of hires from about 59 to 48 percent. Below that threshold the two groups of managers hired almost identically.

Rivera's study of elite professional service firms rests on 120 interviews with employers and observation of a hiring committee. Employers sought candidates who were culturally similar to themselves in leisure pursuits, experiences and self-presentation, and she reports those concerns often outweighing concerns about absolute productivity. The resemblance doing the work there is cultural rather than demographic.

replication.headline: Similarity raises liking in the laboratory at r = .47, and two studies of structured job interviews covering 12,203 and 19,931 applicants find no interviewer-applicant similarity effect at all.
replication.detail:
Montoya, Horton and Kirchner meta-analysed 460 effect sizes from 313 laboratory and field investigations. Actual similarity correlated with attraction at r = .47 and perceived similarity at r = .39. The breakdown by stage is the useful part. Actual similarity predicted attraction in no-interaction and short-interaction studies, fell once any interaction had occurred, and was not significant in existing relationships. Perceived similarity predicted attraction at every stage. An earlier manuscript by the same three authors, hosted on Horton's university page under the filename of the published article but carrying a different title and a smaller dataset of 385 effect sizes from 293 investigations, cuts the literature by setting instead. It reports r = .536 overall, r = .506 in laboratory studies, 95% CI [.425, .586], and r = .150 in field studies. Applying a publication-bias weight function to the field studies moved the mean from 0.152 to 0.029, an attenuation the authors put at about 81 percent, and left the field effect non-significant, z = 1.37, p = .17. The laboratory funnel plot showed no comparable asymmetry.

The workplace tests run against the term. Sacco, Scheu, Ryan and Schmitt analysed one-on-one highly structured college recruiting interviews with 708 interviewers and 12,203 applicants across seven job families. Hierarchical linear models gave no evidence of race or sex similarity effects, while D-scores and analysis of variance at the individual level did give them, which is a finding about levels of analysis before it is a finding about bias. McCarthy, Van Iddekinge and Campion put the same question to 19,931 applicants and 207 interviewers for a managerial post at one large organisation. Neither applicant demographics nor applicant-interviewer similarity moved interview ratings, effect sizes sat consistently below .10, and pseudo R-squared values were zero. The one significant main effect was small: women scored above men by d = .03 to .04. Both sets of authors attribute the null to interview structure, which leaves little to the interviewer's discretion.

study.cite: Montoya, R. M., Horton, R. S., & Kirchner, J. (2008). Is actual similarity necessary for attraction? A meta-analysis of actual and perceived similarity. Journal of Social and Personal Relationships, 25(6), 889-922.

replicated.weighting: actual similarity, 460 effect sizes from 313 investigations

limits:
The name has no located research base, and that is the first limit. Searches covered Crossref title and bibliographic queries, PubMed, PubMed Central and web search. OpenAlex and Semantic Scholar were tried and returned rate-limit errors rather than results. Wikipedia's article on affinity bias names no coiner and gives no citation for the term's history. Where the phrase does appear in indexed scholarship it usually means something unrelated, from ligand binding to graph neural networks.

Byrne's 1961 paper was not read. Its design and its effect size on this page are taken from Greenwald and Pettigrew's description of it, and no interval for the d of 3.40 is available at that remove. The published Montoya meta-analysis sits behind a SAGE paywall that returned HTTP 403; the figures quoted here come from the abstract carried by Crossref, which reports no confidence intervals. The earlier manuscript version was read in full, and whether its publication-bias analysis survived into the published article could not be checked, so the two are kept apart above. Giuliano and colleagues' figures come from the September 2006 working paper hosted at Berkeley, whose abstract matches the published one; the authors state they cannot disclose exact sample sizes because the employer is anonymous. Rivera's article is described from its abstract only. No meta-analysis of similar-to-me effects in employment interviews was found in these searches, so the two large null studies are reported as what was found rather than as the whole of that literature.
misreadings:
The hiring audit studies are the evidence usually produced, and they do not measure affinity. Bertrand and Mullainathan sent fictitious CVs carrying White-sounding and African-American-sounding names to newspaper advertisements in Boston and Chicago, and White names drew 50 percent more callbacks. Quillian, Pager, Hexel and Midtboen pooled every available field experiment of hiring discrimination against African Americans or Latinos, 28 studies representing 55,842 applications for 26,326 positions, and found Whites receiving on average 36 percent more callbacks than African Americans and 24 percent more than Latinos, with no change against African Americans since 1989. None of that shows recruiters favouring their own. Greenwald and Pettigrew, who argue the favouritism case, say so in a footnote: audit studies do not systematically report the race or ethnicity of the hiring managers, so whether the pattern varies with the manager's own group is unknown.

Giuliano, Levine and Leonard did have the manager's race, and their own reading is not the convenient one. They tested four explanations for their result and could rule none out cleanly. They found no evidence that segregated recruiting networks or efficiency drove it, while noting their tests had low power against those explanations. Their strongest positive finding on mechanism was that many White job-seekers appear to avoid working for non-White managers. An own-group hiring pattern can be produced by who applies as well as by who the manager likes.

A third reading treats affinity bias as a mechanism distinct from in-group favouritism. Greenwald and Pettigrew treat similarity-attraction and the minimal group paradigm as two lines of evidence for a single thesis, that favouritism rather than hostility drives most contemporary discrimination.

A fourth treats demographic resemblance as the strongest form of the effect. Rivera's elite firms sorted on leisure and self-presentation. Giuliano's Hispanic manager effect appeared only where Hispanics made up at least 30 percent of the local population and vanished below it, so in the one dataset here that could test the demographic version, it was conditional on context.

sources.text: Byrne, D. (1961). Interpersonal attraction and attitude similarity. The Journal of Abnormal and Social Psychology, 62(3), 713-715. Named as the origin; not read for this entry, and its design and effect size here come from Greenwald and Pettigrew's description.

Greenwald, A. G., & Pettigrew, T. F. (2014). With malice toward none and charity for some: Ingroup favoritism enables discrimination. American Psychologist, 69(7), 669-684. Full text read from the author's hosted copy; the phrase 'affinity bias' does not appear in it.

Montoya, R. M., Horton, R. S., & Kirchner, J. (2008). Is actual similarity necessary for attraction? A meta-analysis of actual and perceived similarity. Journal of Social and Personal Relationships, 25(6), 889-922. Paywalled; the figures here come from the abstract carried by Crossref.

Montoya, R. M., Horton, R. S., & Kirchner, J. Does similarity always lead to attraction? A quantitative research synthesis of the similarity effect. Undated manuscript hosted on Horton's Wabash College page under the filename of the 2008 article. Read in full; it reports 385 effect sizes from 293 investigations and is the source of the laboratory, field and publication-bias figures on this page.
Rand, T. M., & Wexley, K. N. (1975). Demonstration of the effect, 'similar to me,' in simulated employment interviews. Psychological Reports, 36(2), 535-544. Described from its abstract at Crossref.

Sacco, J. M., Scheu, C. R., Ryan, A. M., & Schmitt, N. (2003). An investigation of race and sex similarity effects in interviews: A multilevel approach to relational demography. Journal of Applied Psychology, 88(5), 852-865. Described from its abstract at PubMed.

McCarthy, J. M., Van Iddekinge, C. H., & Campion, M. A. (2010). Are highly structured job interviews resistant to demographic similarity effects? Personnel Psychology, 63(2), 325-359. Full text read from the hosted copy at Rotman.

Giuliano, L., Levine, D. I., & Leonard, J. (2009). Manager race and the race of new hires. Journal of Labor Economics, 27(4), 589-631. Read as the September 2006 working paper hosted at Berkeley, whose abstract matches the published one.
Rivera, L. A. (2012). Hiring as cultural matching: The case of elite professional service firms. American Sociological Review, 77(6), 999-1022. Described from its abstract at Crossref.

Bertrand, M., & Mullainathan, S. (2004). Are Emily and Greg more employable than Lakisha and Jamal? A field experiment on labor market discrimination. American Economic Review, 94(4), 991-1013. Described from its abstract at Crossref.

Quillian, L., Pager, D., Hexel, O., & Midtboen, A. H. (2017). Meta-analysis of field experiments shows no change in racial discrimination in hiring over time. Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, 114(41), 10870-10875. Described from its abstract at PubMed.

Pompian, M. M. (2012). Affinity bias. In Behavioral Finance and Wealth Management, 253-260. The earliest indexed scholarly use of the exact phrase found in these searches, in an unrelated sense; the chapter itself was not read.

Buzanowska, M., & Rensel, M. (2023). Get your diverse team to outperform: Navigating through affinity bias. Management in Healthcare: A Peer-Reviewed Journal, 8(1), 16. Cited as an example of where the term lives; not read.
Westover, J. (2024). Affinity Bias: An Overlook Threat to Diversity, Equity and Inclusion Efforts. Human Capital Leadership Review, 15(2). Cited as an example of where the term lives; not read.
